analysis.title: US September Jobs Preview
key_insights: Consensus for September nonfarm payrolls (due 2 October 2026, 08:30 ET) is +98K, versus 162K reported for August. Private payrolls are expected at +85K versus 127K prior. The 3-month average is 71K, the 6-month average 107K and the 12-month average 50K.
Many analysts argue the August upside surprise was helped by generous seasonal adjustments, so a correction is possible in the September report.

Barclays says its usual claims-based models point to strong gains but alternative indicators suggest more modest growth, with seasonal adjustment the key risk. Using August 2025 seasonal factors, August payrolls would have shown a 74k fall rather than a 162k rise. Barclays expects August to be revised down, which would raise upside risk to September. Little revision would point to a September print below 50k.

The unemployment rate is expected to hold at 4.1%. September FOMC participants lowered their end-2026 jobless rate view to 4.1% from 4.3%. The Chicago Fed's final real-time forecast for September was 4.10% versus 4.14% in August. Some see a small downside risk to the rate because continuing claims fell.

Average hourly earnings are expected at +0.3% M/M (prior 0.3%) and 3.2% Y/Y (prior 3.1%). Some analysts say a calendar quirk might cap hourly earnings. The average workweek is expected at 34.3 hours, down from 34.4.
Claims were low across the survey window. Initial claims were 198k versus 207k in the August window, and continuing claims fell to 1.719mln from 1.771mln.

ADP private payrolls were 90K in September against 70K expected and 38K prior. Hiring accelerated for the first time since May, led by education and health care and leisure and hospitality. Financial activities and professional and business services were weak. Pay growth for job stayers was 4.4% Y/Y and for job changers 7.3% Y/Y, both unchanged.
Revelio's Public Labor Statistics showed +56.9K jobs in September versus a revised-up 40.6K in August. Gains were led by Public Administration, Health Care and Social Assistance, and Construction.

Challenger job cuts were 43,281 in September (-18% M/M, -20% Y/Y), the lowest September total since 2022. Year-to-date cuts of 573,195 are down 39%. Technology led with 10,799 cuts and AI was the leading reason given. Hiring plans rose to 90,787 but are down 23% Y/Y and the lowest for a September since 2011.

S&P Global's flash PMI showed composite employment rising at the fastest rate since June 2022, and manufacturing jobs growth the strongest since February 2021. Firms reported growing difficulty finding staff and rising wage pressure. ISM manufacturing employment rose 1.5 points to 52.7, with eight of 18 industries reporting employment growth and six reporting decreases.

Conference Board consumer confidence showed a softer labour market. Jobs 'plentiful' slipped to 23.6 from 24.5 and 'hard to get' rose to 21.9 from 20.3, narrowing the differential by 2.5 points to +1.7. Net expectations for jobs six months ahead fell 3.1 points to -14.4.

Fed officials broadly describe the labour market as stable and near full employment, with the focus on persistent, broad-based inflation. Barr, Musalem and Paulson have signalled further hikes may be needed. Williams sees another hike by year-end as reasonable and Collins has one more pencilled in this year. Williams also sees no need for urgency after the September hike.

Market pricing for an October Fed hike has fallen to around 34% from roughly 70% last week, after a softer-than-expected August PCE. The jobs data will shape this further, and another CPI and PPI report comes before the 28 October FOMC. The ISM services index will not be released until after the jobs report.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Consensus is well below August's 162K. A print above consensus would add to hike risk, while a downward revision to August would raise upside risk to September.
Analysts say seasonal adjustments flattered the figure, and Barclays expects a downward revision.
Private hiring is expected to slow from August.
Expected unchanged. The Chicago Fed forecast and falling continuing claims suggest a risk of a small decline.
A calendar quirk might cap the monthly reading.
A small uptick in annual wage growth is expected.
Beat expectations and marked the first acceleration in hiring since May.

A faster pace than August's revised 40.6K.

risk_factors: Seasonal adjustment distortion could cause a downward revision to August payrolls and make the September print unreliable.
If August is not revised, Barclays says a September print below 50k is likely.
Consumer expectations for jobs six months ahead are worsening while business surveys are strong, so the signals conflict.
Firms report wage pressure and higher fuel and transport costs, which feed Fed concerns about persistent inflation.
A strong jobs print could revive October rate hike pricing, which has fallen to around 34%.
geopolitical: Challenger cited the war in Iran, along with high energy costs and rate hikes, as factors in job cuts and hiring plans.
